query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled 0.5 atomic percent interstitial carbon into a single-phase FCC CoNiV high-entropy alloy will improve its mechanical durability, reduce room-temperature creep, and enhance corrosion resistance for aerospace fastener applications.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic, single-phase FCC CoNiV medium-entropy alloy fabricated using conventional casting methods with negligible interstitial carbon.
generation.intervention: Dope the HEA during fabrication with 0.5 at% carbon, ensuring even interstitial distribution.
generation.conditions: Standard room temperature conditions with mechanical loading (tensile and creep tests) and exposure to corrosion tests in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.
generation.structural_mediator: The addition of interstitial carbon increases solid-solution strengthening and promotes the formation of nano-scale twins and stacking faults that refine the microstructure and serve as nucleation sites for a denser, uniform passivation layer.
generation.mechanism: Interstitial carbon enhances the lattice distortion and activates additional deformation mechanisms (such as nano-twinning), thereby increasing yield strength and impeding dislocation motion under sustained load (improving creep resistance), while also facilitating the development of a stable oxide film that protects against corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the carbon-free baseline, the carbon-doped alloy should display a 15–25% increase in tensile yield strength, at least a 20% reduction in room-temperature creep strain under a fixed load, and a reduction in corrosion current density by roughly 20% as measured by potentiodynamic tests.
generation.baseline: The identical CoNiV HEA produced without interstitial carbon, exhibiting lower strength and higher susceptibility to creep and corrosion.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected for carbon additions around 0.5 at%; higher carbon levels could lead to embrittlement or deleterious phase formation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise influence of carbon on passivation behavior and its interplay with the alloy’s microstructure require careful optimization; the dose sensitivity remains a key uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of CoNiV HEA specimens: one set with standard processing (no added carbon) and one with 0.5 at% carbon added during casting. Subject both sets to room-temperature tensile tests, sustained load creep experiments, and corrosion testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.
measurements: Creep strain under a set load at room temperature
Corrosion current density via potentiodynamic polarization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped specimens do not exhibit at least a 15% improvement in yield strength, a measurable (≥20%) reduction in creep strain, and enhanced corrosion resistance (20% lower corrosion current density) compared to the undoped samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: First, the addition of interstitial carbon into a recently developed TRIP-DP-HEA leads to an increase in stacking fault energy and hence phase stability. Tuning the stability of the face-centered cubic (f.c.c.) matrix phase in the dual-phase structure to a critical point triggers the twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) effect while maintaining the TRIP effect, thereby further improving the alloy’s strain-hardening ability,. Second, HEAs benefit profoundly from interstitial solid solution strengthening instead of only the established massive solid solution strengthening provided by its multiple principle elements,. This is due to the circumstance that carbon, nitrogen and other interstitials lead to much higher lattice distortions than substitutional elements which strongly affects their interaction with dislocations,. We produced the interstitial HEA (iHEA) by melting and casting in a vacuum induction furnace using pure metals and carbon with nominal composition Fe49.5Mn30Co10Cr10C0.5 (at%). The cast alloy was hot-rolled, homogenized and water-quenched. Further grain refinement was achieved by cold-rolling and annealing in Ar atmosphere. The bulk chemical composition of the iHEA mea

The improved mechanical properties (Fig. 3) and the associated multiple deformation mechanisms (Fig. 4) confirm the success of the new design approach, and its potential economic viability since interstitial alloying elements are much cheaper compared to substitutional alloying elements. The new interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEAs unify all known metallurgical strengthening effects in one single bulk material: i) massive substitutional solid solution strengthening due to multiple principle elements (i.e., Fe, Mn, Co and Cr); ii) interstitial solid solution strengthening by carbon; iii) micro-composite effect from dual-phase structure; iv) nano-particle strengthening from nano-carbides (Figs 2b and 4c); v) nano-twinning induced plasticity effect (TWIP) (Fig. 4b); vi) displacive transformation induced plasticity effect (TRIP) (Fig. 4a); vii) formation of stacking faults (Fig. 4b); viii) grain size reduction (increased grain boundary density); and dislocation hardening (Fig. 4b).

In this work, we present an equiatomic CoNiV MEA, which maintains its good mechanical performance under the impact of hydrogen, i.e., the material under investigation shows no obvious hydrogen embrittlement at a temperature of 300 K and a strain rate of 10−4 s−1, and it has good corrosion resistance when exposed to acidic environments. This property synergy, balancing strength, ductility, corrosion, and hydrogen embrittlement, is realized by four main effects: The alloy’s solid solution hardened single face-centered cubic (f.c.c.) phase structure, devoid of any precipitations, provides both, (1) low hydrogen diffusivity and (2) absence of local electrochemical potential gradients. (3) The solute hydrogen in the bulk alloy matrix leads to the formation of deformation twins which impede crack propagation during slow strain rate tensile testing,. (4) The formation of an oxide barrier film with low concentrations of point defects, i.e., metal and oxygen vacancies and metal interstitials, and low content of Co- and Ni-containing hydroxides on the alloy surface in sulfuric acid solution acts as an efficient barrier against oxygen transport, thereby enhancing corrosion resistance. papers.title: New HfNbTaTiZr High-Entropy Alloy Coatings Produced by Electrospark Deposition with High Corrosion Resistance.
papers.system: HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy coatings on stainless steel
papers.approach: Mechanical alloying of elemental powders followed by spark plasma sintering and electrospark deposition (ESD) under an argon shield to produce low-oxygen, high-purity coatings.
papers.findings: The coatings show high corrosion resistance in 3.5% NaCl solution, with good adhesion and improved hardness relative to the substrate.
papers.mechanism: Rapid cooling during ESD in an argon atmosphere minimizes oxidation and produces a homogeneous microstructure that enhances passivation and limits corrosive attack.

papers.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy.
papers.system: Precipitation strengthened HEA fabricated by selective laser melting
papers.approach: Post heat treatment with a controlled, reduced cooling rate to encourage coarsening of γ′ precipitates and induce serrated grain boundaries (SEGB).
papers.findings: At 650°C, serrated grain boundaries improved tensile fracture strain by a factor of 3.5 and extended creep rupture life by a factor of 400 compared to a straight grain boundary morphology.
papers.mechanism: The SEGB distributes strain more evenly, reducing local strain concentration at triple junctions and impeding intergranular crack propagation.

papers.title: A strong and ductile medium-entropy alloy resists hydrogen embrittlement and corrosion.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoNiV medium-entropy alloy with a single FCC solid solution
papers.approach: Alloy design with controlled composition to avoid precipitates, promoting a dense oxide film formation and enabling deformation twinning under strain.
papers.findings: Exhibits high strength, excellent ductility (elongation >90%), low hydrogen diffusivity, and high corrosion resistance in dilute sulfuric acid.
papers.mechanism: A combination of low internal micromechanical contrast, effective twin-induced strain distribution, and formation of a protective oxide barrier minimizes hydrogen uptake and corrosion.

papers.title: The High Temperature Tensile and Creep Behaviors of High Entropy Superalloy.
papers.system: Precipitation strengthened high entropy superalloy (HESA) with FCC matrix and L12 γ′ precipitates
papers.approach: Design incorporating a high volume fraction of stable γ′ precipitates to achieve high tensile and creep strength, with discussion on minor alloying additions.
papers.findings: The alloy achieves high tensile yield strengths from room temperature to elevated temperatures and a creep rupture life at 982°C comparable to Ni-based superalloys.
papers.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening via high γ′ volume, positive lattice misfit promoting raft formation, and reduced stacking fault energy contribute to both high strength and creep resistance.

papers.title: Effects of Mo Addition on Microstructure and Corrosion Resistance of Cr25-xCo25Ni25Fe25Mo_x High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: CrCoNiFe high-entropy alloys processed via directed energy deposition (DED) with variable Mo content
papers.approach: Substitutional alloying by adding controlled amounts (5–10%) of Mo during powder-based DED processing.
papers.findings: Addition of Mo leads to increases in yield strength and ultimate tensile strength (up to 32.5% increase in YS at 10% Mo) and enhances corrosion resistance in 3.5% NaCl solutions.
papers.mechanism: Mo atoms segregate at grain boundaries and within σ phase particles, refining microstructure, enhancing passivation film formation, and serving as physical obstacles to dislocation and grain boundary motion.

papers.title: Investigation of the Micromechanical Behavior of a Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 (at.%) High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 HEA intended for high strength with adjustable corrosion properties
papers.approach: Combined experimental testing and simulation to assess the effect of varying Mo content on hardness and modulus.
papers.findings: Increases in Mo increase both hardness and elastic modulus linearly, with the alloy at 20% Mo demonstrating good corrosion resistance, although ductility may decrease at high Mo content.
papers.mechanism: Mo acts as a strengthening agent via solid-solution effects and lattice distortion, contributing to enhanced mechanical performance and corrosion resistance.

established: Electrospark deposition can produce HEA coatings with superior corrosion resistance by minimizing oxidation through rapid cooling and protective atmospheres.
Controlled microstructural modifications, such as inducing serrated grain boundary morphologies via tailored heat treatments, enhance tensile properties and creep resistance.

Alloying additions like molybdenum (Mo) improve mechanical performance and corrosion resistance in HEAs by modifying the microstructure, refining grains, and promoting robust passivation layer formation.

approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced corrosion resistance with improved surface adhesion and hardness; effective for localized repair and protection.

approaches_tried.approach: Post heat treatment to induce serrated grain boundaries
approaches_tried.outcome: Significant improvements in tensile ductility and creep rupture life at elevated temperatures; mechanism focused on strain distribution.

approaches_tried.approach: Mo addition via directed energy deposition
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced yield and ultimate tensile strengths along with improved corrosion resistance in saline environments; potential for microstructural refinement.

mechanisms: Enhanced passivation via formation of stable oxide films (facilitated by Mo segregation).
Microstructural refinement through grain boundary engineering (e.g., serrated grain boundaries reducing local stress concentrations).
Precipitation strengthening and raft formation of ordered phases (γ′) contributing to yield strength and creep resistance.
Solid-solution strengthening combined with lattice distortion from interstitial and substitutional alloying.
disagreements: While Mo addition improves mechanical strength and corrosion resistance, higher levels may decrease ductility, posing a trade-off.

The relative benefits of inducing serrated grain boundaries versus chemical alloying (e.g., Mo addition) remain to be combined or contrasted directly, particularly regarding room‐temperature creep behavior in aerospace settings.
open_questions: Can a single intervention, such as targeted Mo addition, simultaneously optimize mechanical durability, room‐temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance in HEAs for aerospace fasteners?
How do microstructural modifications (e.g., serrated grain boundaries) interact with chemical interventions (e.g., Mo addition) in affecting the long-term performance of aerospace fasteners?
What are the precise contributions of each mechanism (passivation, grain boundary reinforcement, precipitation strengthening) at room temperature under sustained loading conditions?
opportunities: Investigate combined processing strategies that merge Mo addition with post heat treatment protocols aimed at inducing serrated grain boundaries.
Explore additive manufacturing techniques (DED, ESD) to precisely control both chemical composition and microstructural features in aerospace-grade HEAs.
Design systematic experiments to evaluate room-temperature creep performance alongside mechanical durability and corrosion resistance in HEAs tailored for aerospace fastener applications.

directions.assessment: Mo addition is supported by several studies demonstrating improved yield strength, passivation formation, and corrosion resistance. Its solid‐solution effect and grain boundary segregation are known to impede dislocation motion and enhance barrier properties. However, excessive Mo can impair ductility, so the intervention must be optimized.

directions.direction: Post heat treatment to induce serrated grain boundaries.
directions.assessment: Controlled slow cooling post solution treatment can coarsen precipitates to interact with grain boundaries and produce a serrated morphology. Evidence shows improvements in tensile ductility and creep properties (albeit tested at elevated temperatures), and the mechanism may extend to room temperature. Feasibility for aerospace fasteners needs targeted verification.

directions.direction: Grain refinement via severe plastic deformation (e.g., cryo-rolling).
directions.assessment: Severe plastic deformation to achieve ultrafine grain sizes can enhance yield strength, reduce creep strain by increasing grain boundary density, and promote more uniform passivation films for better corrosion resistance. The physics of grain boundary strengthening and passivation is well established, though care must be taken to avoid embrittlement.

A small, controlled addition of interstitial carbon can boost solid-solution strengthening and trigger nano-twinning or stacking-fault formation. This can enhance mechanical durability and improve corrosion resistance via a more robust oxide or passivation layer. However, carbon levels must be kept low to prevent embrittlement.

directions.direction: Surface modification via electrospark deposition of HEA coatings.
directions.assessment: Deposition of a HEA coating using electrospark processing enhances surface hardness and corrosion resistance by utilizing rapid cooling in protective atmospheres. While beneficial for surface-related degradation, its effects on overall bulk mechanical durability and room-temperature creep resistance may be less direct for aerospace fasteners.

candidates.hypothesis: Adding 5 wt% Mo to a baseline CrCoNiFe high‐entropy alloy processed via directed energy deposition will improve mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance in aerospace fastener applications.
candidates.intervention: Incorporate 5 wt% Mo by substituting part of one constituent during powder blending before DED processing.

candidates.hypothesis: A controlled slow-cooling post heat treatment that induces serrated grain boundaries in a precipitation-strengthened HEA will enhance mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance for aerospace fasteners.
candidates.intervention: Apply a post solution heat treatment followed by a slow cooling process (e.g., cooling over 2 hours) to promote the formation of serrated grain boundaries via controlled coarsening of γ′ precipitates.

candidates.hypothesis: Severe plastic deformation by cryo-rolling to achieve an ultrafine grain structure in a bulk HEA will enhance its mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance in aerospace fasteners.
candidates.intervention: Subject the HEA to severe plastic deformation by cryo-rolling with a reduction of at least 75% to induce ultrafine grain sizes.
